p.src: 7 (p. xxxv) Neither Emily nor Anne was learned: Emily was, in fact, very learned. Like her siblings, she had access from childhood to a wide variety of books and periodicals, which she absorbed. Besides acquiring a knowledge of French and German, she was also well versed in both Latin and Greek, as well as in classical literature—those learned fields that were predominantly the purview of men at the time. M. Heger, the director of the Pensionnat Heger in Brussels, where Emily and Charlotte studied in 1842, characterized Emily as having “ ‘a head for logic, and a capability of argument, unusual in a man, and rare indeed in a woman’ ” (quoted in Barker, The Brontës, p. 392; see “For Further Reading”).
